subtitle: SNMP management objects for monitoring network traffic flows.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a standard way to read traffic flow statistics from network meters using SNMP, the Internet's standard management protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The Meter MIB defines managed objects (data points) that network meters expose so administrators can query them via SNMP to learn about traffic flows, including sources, destinations, and traffic volumes.
tldr.outcome: This experimental specification allowed devices to report traffic measurements in a standardized way, but it was later replaced by RFC 2720 with a more complete framework.

sections.title: Network Management and MIBs
sections.content:
This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for use with SNMP, the protocol that network administrators use to monitor and control devices on the Internet. A MIB is a collection of data points that a device exposes so that managers can read and sometimes change them remotely.

RFC 2064 specifically defines the MIB objects for Traffic Flow Measurement devices (often called meters), which observe network traffic and build up statistics about where traffic flows from and to. This allows administrators to gather network usage data from devices using SNMP queries.
sections.eli5: A MIB is like a numbered list of questions you can ask a network device. This RFC creates questions for traffic meters so managers can ask them about the traffic they see.

sections.title: Traffic Flow Concepts
sections.content:
The Meter MIB organizes traffic flows around several key concepts. A flow is identified by a set of attributes at different layers of the network stack: addresses at the link layer (like MAC addresses for Ethernet), network layer (like IP addresses), and transport layer (like TCP or UDP ports), plus optional subscriber identifiers for billing.

The MIB breaks into four main parts: control variables that let managers configure the meter, the flows table containing traffic statistics, rules that determine what gets measured, and conformance statements that explain what parts a meter must implement. This modular design lets different meters implement different feature sets.
sections.eli5: Traffic flows are described by where they come from and where they go, at several levels (like Ethernet addresses, IP addresses, and port numbers). Managers set up rules for what to count, and the meter reports back the statistics.

sections.title: Objects and Data Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines textual conventions (custom data types) for the various pieces of information a meter needs to track. AddressType specifies what kind of address field is being used (IP, NSAP, IEEE 802 MAC, IPX, AppleTalk, or DECnet). PeerAddress and TransportAddress hold the actual address values in the format appropriate to their type.

FlowAttributeNumber identifies which attribute is being accessed in a flow record, covering 41 different possible attributes including source and destination addresses at multiple layers, octet and packet counts in both directions, and activity timestamps. RuleAttributeNumber lists which attributes can be tested in rule conditions, and ActionNumber defines the opcodes that rule conditions can execute (such as count, assign, goto, or gosub for subroutine calls).
sections.eli5: The RFC carefully defines what types of information can be stored: which kinds of addresses (IP, Ethernet, etc.), what counters and timestamps track about each flow, and what actions rules can take.

sections.title: Rule Sets and Data Collection
sections.content:
Managers interact with the meter through three control tables. The flowRuleSetInfoTable manages rule sets: before loading rules, a manager creates a row in this table marked 'createAndWait' and later sets it to 'active' when ready. flowReaderInfoTable is used by data collectors to register themselves and signal which flows they have already collected; the meter does not free a flow's memory until all registered readers have fetched its data.

The flowManagerInfoTable allows managers to register and then control which rule set the meter is running. To reduce SNMP overhead when retrieving large numbers of flows, the MIB provides a TimeFilter index that, combined with SNMP GetBulk requests, lets collectors fetch only flows that have changed since the last read. An alternative approach uses a flowColumnActivityTable that returns data for an entire column of the flow table in a single opaque object.
sections.eli5: Managers send commands to the meter by creating rows in tables and setting flags, then download rule sets that tell the meter what to count. When collecting data, managers can ask for just the new or changed traffic records to avoid transferring too much data.

sections.title: Standardization and Status
sections.content:
The Meter MIB was first developed and tested using SNMPv1 (the original SNMP protocol) and later converted to SNMPv2 (which added more data types and cleaner language). The RFC was published as Experimental, reflecting that the architecture and objects were still being refined by the Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement (RTFM) Working Group.

RFC 2064 established the foundational MIB structure for traffic measurement but was superseded by RFC 2720, which provided a more complete and mature specification. Today, network operators typically use this or similar traffic flow measurement standards for network monitoring and capacity planning.
sections.eli5: This was an experimental standard to let network devices report traffic statistics using SNMP. A later RFC improved on it, but the basic ideas about tracking flows and using rules to measure traffic stayed the same.
